chunks.document_content: In vitro: Human retinal microvascular endothelial cells (HRMECs); nor­ mal conditions Finding Relevant to EGFR Ref Several EGFR inhibitors with established clinical pro­ files might represent attractive repurposing candidates for DR. The small-molecule inhibitors gefitinib and erlo­ tinib, FDA-approved for NSCLC since the early 2000s [160, 161], have demonstrated efficacy in preclinical DR models (Table 1, Fig. 4), as has the FDA-approved monoclonal antibody cetuximab [91, 162]. However, repurposing must account for the dual physiological and pathological roles of EGFR in the eye, necessitating temporally and spatially controlled delivery to optimize efficacy and limit systemic exposure. While the known adverse effects of systemic EGFR inhibition, including dermatological toxicity and diarrhea, are generally man­ ageable in oncology, they present meaningful challenges in the setting of chronic ocular disease. a key complementary strand of development alongside mechanistic validation of EGFR as a therapeutic target in a chronic, multifactorial disease such as DR. A further rationale for EGFR-targeted therapy lies in its mechanistic convergence with VEGF signaling. Sub­ stantial crosstalk exists between HB-EGF/EGFR and VEGF pathways, whereby EGFR activation converges on shared downstream effectors to upregulate VEGF expres­ sion, establishing a self-amplifying pro-angiogenic feed-forward loop (Fig. 4). This interdependence suggests that VEGF blockade alone may incompletely suppress angio­ genic signaling, particularly in persistent or recurrent disease. Combined EGFR and VEGF inhibition could therefore modulate a broader network of angiogenic, and inflammatory pathways implicated in DR progression. While dual EGFR/VEGF inhibition is FDA-approved in NSCLC [167], this approval is disease- and mutation-specific and does not constitute evidence of retinal effi­ cacy or safety; independent clinical investigation in the retinal context would therefore be required before con­ clusions regarding therapeutic benefit can be drawn. From a translational perspective, local intravitreal delivery of EGFR-targeted therapies represents a strategi­ cally attractive approach that could circumvent the sys­ temic toxicity associated with oral or intravenous EGFR inhibitors. Preclinical studies have already established the feasibility of this approach, demonstrating that intravit­ real administration of small-molecule EGFR inhibitors [49, 94, 163] and neutralizing antibodies directed against EGFR ligands, including HB-EGF [99], can achieve thera­ peutically relevant target engagement within the retina without systemic exposure. Interestingly, the encapsula­ tion of EGFR inhibitors within sustained-release polymer nanospheres has provided early proof-of-concept for this delivery paradigm, with Robinson et al. demonstrating enhanced optic neuronal regeneration in a nerve-crush injury model [163], findings that underscore the capac­ ity of optimized intraocular pharmacokinetics to enhance therapeutic efficacy while preserving ocular safety. Additional angiogenic pathways also warrant con­ sideration as co-targets. Angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2), a key mediator of vascular destabilization and inflammation, is upregulated in DR and acts permissively to amplify growth factor-driven angiogenesis downstream of both VEGF and EGFR [168]. The recent FDA approval of Faricimab, a bispecific antibody targeting Ang-2 and VEGF-A, establishes a clinical precedent for multi-target approaches in ocular disease [169], and underscores the biological plausibility of next-generation fusion proteins directed against EGFR in combination with VEGF-A and/or Ang-2. By addressing multiple pathological mech­ anisms simultaneously, such strategies could comple­ ment or reduce reliance on adjunctive treatments such as pan-retinal photocoagulation, thereby minimizing asso­ ciated complications including choroidal effusion, retinal detachment, and macular edema [170].
